meta.title: Fine-tuning vs RAG vs Prompting
meta.thesis: Prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, and fine-tuning solve different adaptation problems: steering behavior at request time, grounding answers in external knowledge, or changing model behavior through training examples.

mentalMap.title: Prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning?
mentalMap.caption: The map compares the three adaptation levers by what kind of problem they solve.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Prompting changes instructions, RAG supplies changing facts, and fine-tuning changes repeated behavior in the model.

nodes.label: Prompting
nodes.sub: Build the simplest useful picture of Fine-tuning vs RAG vs Prompting.
nodes.what: Prompting changes behavior by changing the visible request.
nodes.relevance: It is the first lever when the model already has the capability.
nodes.orient: Best for instructions, roles, examples, output shape, and fast iteration.

nodes.label: RAG
nodes.sub: See the moving parts and how they interact.
nodes.what: RAG supplies evidence at request time.
nodes.relevance: It avoids retraining when facts change or need citations.
nodes.orient: Best for private, recent, or large knowledge that should stay external.

nodes.label: Fine-tuning
nodes.sub: Make the choices that change quality, cost, or risk.
nodes.what: Fine-tuning updates model weights for a narrower behavior.
nodes.relevance: It helps when prompting is too brittle and facts are not the issue.
nodes.orient: Best for stable repeated behavior learned from representative examples.

nodes.label: Decision criteria
nodes.sub: Connect the concept to a small practical artifact.
nodes.what: Criteria prevent choosing the fanciest lever by default.
nodes.relevance: They guide beginners toward the smallest reliable change.
nodes.orient: Compare freshness, behavior stability, cost, eval readiness, and risk.

nodes.label: Recommendation
nodes.sub: Use active recall and a decision checklist to make it stick.
nodes.what: The final choice maps problem type to adaptation method.
nodes.relevance: It turns the comparison into an actionable next step.
nodes.orient: Pick the smallest lever that solves the actual failure mode.

modules.title: The three levers solve different failures
modules.sub: Start by diagnosing the adaptation problem before choosing a method.
modules.summary: A beginner mistake is using the most expensive lever first. The real question is whether the failure is instruction, knowledge, or learned behavior.
objectives: Avoid using fine-tuning for missing facts.

blocks.title: Adaptation begins with failure diagnosis

spans.text: Prompting, RAG, and fine-tuning all change model behavior, but they act at different layers. Prompting changes the visible instructions. RAG changes the evidence sent with the request. Fine-tuning changes weights through training examples.
Problem anchor: a refund assistant is polite but cites old policy, formats answers inconsistently, and sometimes misroutes escalation cases. One lever will not fix all three failures.
Before reading on, predict: which lever should handle a policy that changes every month?

blocks.analogy: The three levers are like editing the recipe card, bringing the right ingredients, or retraining the cook.

blocks.title: Worked diagnosis: three failures, three levers

items.text: Wrong tone: try prompting and examples first.
Stale refund rule: use RAG over the current policy source.
Repeated escalation-label mistake across many examples: consider fine-tuning after evals prove the pattern.

blocks.title: Check diagnosis
blocks.prompt: Which lever is usually best for changing facts?

options.text: Fine-tuning, because all knowledge should live in weights.
RAG, because facts can stay external and update without retraining.
Temperature, because it makes facts current.

blocks.explanation: Changing knowledge is a retrieval problem more often than a training problem.

modules.title: Prompting is the fastest behavior lever
modules.sub: First test whether better instructions and examples solve the issue.
modules.summary: Prompting is best for task framing, tone, format, refusal policy, and context use when the model already has the capability.
objectives: Write a prompt as a testable interface.
Know when prompting is too brittle.

blocks.title: Prompts steer visible behavior

spans.text: A prompt can define role, task, constraints, examples, context boundaries, and output shape. It is the cheapest lever to change and the easiest to evaluate.
Prompting fails when the model lacks needed evidence, the behavior is too frequent and brittle, or the output requires a hard schema better enforced by structured outputs.

blocks.analogy: A prompt is a checklist on the counter; it helps if the cook already knows how to cook.

blocks.title: Complete prompt slice for refund tone

spans.text: Role: support assistant. Context: current retrieved refund policy will appear below. Task: answer in three short bullets. Constraints: do not invent policy, cite the source section, and ask for invoice ID if missing. Output: `answer`, `source_section`, `missing_info`.
This prompt is useful before fine-tuning because it creates an eval target. If it works reliably, training is unnecessary.

blocks.title: Check prompting
blocks.prompt: When should prompting be tried first?

options.text: When the app needs private changing policy text.
When the model has the capability and needs clearer instructions, examples, or format.
When hundreds of labeled examples already prove a stable model-weight change is needed.

blocks.explanation: Prompting is the fastest first lever for steerable behavior.

modules.title: RAG keeps knowledge outside weights
modules.sub: Use retrieval when correctness depends on current or private sources.
modules.summary: RAG answers with external evidence. It is the right lever when the facts should be updated, cited, or access-controlled.
objectives: Explain why RAG is not fine-tuning.

blocks.title: RAG supplies evidence at request time

spans.text: RAG loads, chunks, indexes, retrieves, and packs evidence for the model to use. The model still writes the answer, but the facts come from the retrieved source pack.
Use RAG for policies, product docs, customer records, internal knowledge, and other material that changes or needs provenance.

blocks.analogy: RAG is an open-book exam: the answer still needs reasoning, but the facts come from the book.

spans.text: The bot says refunds are available for 60 days because that pattern appeared in old examples. The policy changed to 30 days. Fine-tuning would bake in another snapshot; RAG can retrieve the current policy section at answer time.

blocks.title: Check RAG

options.text: The model cannot parse JSON syntax.
Retriever misses the policy paragraph, so generation answers from weak or wrong evidence.
The training learning rate is too high.

blocks.explanation: RAG quality depends on retrieval, metadata, and grounding as well as generation.

modules.title: Fine-tuning teaches stable repeated behavior
modules.sub: Train only after prompting and evals reveal a durable pattern.
modules.summary: Fine-tuning is for frequent stable behavior, format, domain shorthand, or task patterns that prompts cannot stabilize.
objectives: Explain why evals come before training.
Avoid training on stale or sensitive facts.

blocks.title: Fine-tuning changes model weights

spans.text: Fine-tuning continues training on examples. The goal is not to add one new fact. The goal is to make a repeated behavior more likely by default: style, labels, tool-argument shape, specialist formatting, or domain shorthand.
The KB verdict is direct: use fine-tuning when repeated behavior should become part of the model, not when the app only needs fresher facts.

blocks.analogy: Fine-tuning is like practice drills; it changes habit, not the current contents of the textbook.

blocks.title: Tiny lever recommender

spans.text: Run this as a tiny model of the mechanism. The point is to predict behavior before trusting the output.

predictThenReveal.answer: It prints stale facts -> RAG, tone or format -> Prompting, and stable repeated label error -> Fine-tuning. The point is root-cause diagnosis before adaptation.

syntax.explains: The small concrete case the example operates on.
The line or function that turns the inputs into behavior.
A visible result so you can check your prediction.

spans.text: When an AI recommends fine-tuning, make it justify the root cause.

items.text: Does it show a prompted baseline and eval suite first?
Does it avoid training on changing policy facts?
Does it define train/validation/test splits and rollback?
Does it compare against RAG and prompting honestly?

modules.title: Head-to-head: choose the smallest lever
modules.sub: End by comparing options across the same criteria.
modules.summary: The final decision should choose the smallest lever that solves the actual failure with acceptable cost and risk.
objectives: Use a decision matrix for adaptation.

blocks.title: Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning

options.name: Prompting

cells.text: Instructions, tone, examples, formatting, refusal policy.
Lowest; fast to edit and test.
Brittle behavior under long or adversarial context.
Use first when capability exists and facts are available.

options.whenToUse: Choose when clearer instructions and examples can solve the behavior.

options.name: RAG

cells.text: Private, changing, cited, or large knowledge.
Medium; needs indexing, retrieval, metadata, evals.
Retriever misses or citations do not support claims.
Use when facts should stay external and current.

options.whenToUse: Choose when the answer depends on current or source-grounded knowledge.

options.name: Fine-tuning

cells.text: Stable repeated behavior learned from examples.
Highest; needs data, training, registry, rollback.
Overfit, stale facts, sensitive data, regressions.
Use after evals show prompting/RAG are insufficient.

options.whenToUse: Choose when durable behavior belongs in weights and examples are representative.

blocks.howToRead: Read the failure first, then choose the smallest lever that addresses that failure.

blocks.title: Completion problem: classify the support bot failures

spans.text: Failure A: “The answer uses last quarter’s policy.” Choose RAG. Failure B: “The tone is too verbose.” Try prompting. Failure C: “The model repeatedly maps `billing_dispute` tickets to `technical_support` despite clear examples.” Consider fine-tuning after evals.

blocks.title: Check the recommendation
blocks.prompt: What is the safest default order?

options.text: Fine-tune first because it is most powerful.
Prompt and evaluate, add RAG for changing facts, fine-tune only for stable repeated behavior.
Use RAG for tone and style only.

modules.decisionItForces: Choose prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning for an adaptation problem.
